 UNM LOBOS BASKETBALL
 Lobos face pivotal résumé tests on road
 New Mexico opens a challenging stretch at Santa Clara before traveling to Wichita State, with early wins critical to its NCAA Tournament hopes
 Lobos players respond to a basket made by Hudson Mayes, right, during the second half against Northern Arizona on Saturday, in the Pit. 
 Mike Sandoval/Journal 
 Geoff Grammer 
 Geoff 
 Grammer 
 Journal Staff Writer 
 Published 
 November 13, 2026 - 7:58 p.m. 
 Modified 
 November 13, 2026 - 11:26 p.m. 
 Saturday
 What: UNM men’s basketball
 Who: New Mexico at Santa Clara
 When: Saturday, 8 p.m.
 Broadcast: ESPN+ (stream), 610 AM/95.9 FM (radio)
 There are no must wins in November. 
 But with the new makeup of the Mountain West conference appearing as though it will pretty much cut in half the number of quality in-conference games it was used to in past years — the types of games the NCAA Tournament Selection Committee hones in on to determine whether a team deserves to be invited to the Big Dance — things got pretty critical pretty fast for Eric Olen’s squad. 
 Starting Saturday night at Santa Clara, the Lobos play back-to-back tournament résumé building opponents — at preseason West Coast Conference favorite Santa Clara on Saturday and at preseason American Conference favorite Wichita State next weekend (Nov. 21). 
 “We talked about it — the level is going up,” UNM coach Eric Olen said. “Really good team on the road. Great opportunity for us — an NCAA tournament team last year (and) certainly that caliber team again this year, and you know we’ll have to do a good job in all the phases to have success.”
 In a more expanded view, after playing three opponents ranked between 227 and 262 in KenPom.com’s national ratings, they now have a stretch of four opponents in the next six games that are rated in the top 80 — Saturday at Santa Clara (71), Nov. 21 at Wichita State (80), Nov. 29 vs. Utah State (42) and Dec. 12 vs. Saint Mary’s (67). 
 The stretch is very much on the radar of national college basketball analysts who understand that despite the NCAA Tournament’s expanded field this year to 76 teams, there is almost no wiggle room left for teams like the Lobos. 
 And as Rob Dauster of the Field of 68 notes, these aren’t merely good opportunities for the Lobos if they win, they are games against the very mid-major programs they are fighting for those select few at-large berths. 
 “As of today, UNM plays six non-conference games against Top 100 opponents,” Dauster told the Journal. “They play four total games against teams ranked inside the top 100 KenPom in league play (UNLV is 100 right now).
 “Those eight extra bids are a carrot for the teams at the top of the league to chase, but the teams they will be competing against for those spots are the teams they are playing in the next two weeks. Not only would a loss be a missed opportunity, but it would be helping out the teams that will take those bids.”
 UNM guard Uriah Tenette (1) moves past Little Rock’s Taj Walters (6) during the University of New Mexico Lobos men's basketball game against the Little Rock Trojans at The Pit in Albuquerque, N.M., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. 
 Chancey Bush/Journal 
 To some, it isn’t a matter of the Lobos proving whether they are a worthy team to play in the NCAA Tournament. They are. 
 But the schedule, through no fault of their own in a current landscape where power conference teams won’t schedule them, doesn’t allow for them to get in without a lot of these November wins under their belt.
 “New Mexico has the goods to be an NCAA Tournament team with a potential top 10 All-American in Jake Hall,” former Journal staffer and longtime national college basketball analyst Andy Katz said. “But to get there they can’t just rely on the Mountain West schedule. They need to handle their business in the non-conference. And the next four games could have a say in their positioning if they are put in an at-large situation.”
 Stop the steal?
 The Lobos have been flourishing on points off turnovers against lesser teams through the first three games. 
 And they are scoring 96.0 points per game as a result — No. 22 out of 365 Division I teams.
 But what happens when a team doesn’t have live ball turnovers setting up transition scoring for the Lobos? What happens when the Lobos’ 11.3 steals per game (No. 27 in the country) aren’t a factor in creating easy offense? 
 Olen remains confident in his team’s scoring, even if the first three opponents weren’t the best litmus test to prove halfcourt offensive efficiency. 
 “I think there are some ways that we haven’t been tested in the regular season yet, and I think that's a good example of one,” Olen acknowledged. “But I think that we certainly are capable of being a very efficient halfcourt offensive team. … 
 “I know we’ve had possessions that get deeper in the shot clock, and we’ve been able to find quality shots. And so we have a lot of confidence in our ability to score in the halfcourt.”
 Series history
 UNM leads the all-time series 6-3 with the Lobos having won the last two, including last season in the Pit. 
 Saturday’s game is the back end of a home-and-home contract that saw the Broncos visit the Pit on Dec. 6, 2025 — a lopsided 98-71 Lobos win. 
 In that game, five Lobos scored in double figures, including a 22-point, six assist, three steal game for point guard Deyton Albury. 
 Geoff Grammer is the Sports Editor of the Journal, a podcaster, columnist, and covers UNM Lobos basketball, among other things. Reach him at ggrammer@abqjournal.com or follow him on Twitter (X) @GeoffGrammer .
